title: Chè Trôi Nước
subtitle: glutinous rice balls in ginger syrup
excerpt: Chè trôi nước are soft, chewy glutinous rice balls filled with sweet mung bean paste, served in a warm ginger syrup and topped with coconut cream. They are a popular Vietnamese dessert with a comforting, warming flavour. This recipe serves 4.
sourceNotes: Chè trôi nước is a Vietnamese adaptation of the Chinese tangyuan, brought to Vietnam through centuries of cultural exchange. The name means 'floating rice balls' as they rise to the surface when cooked.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze uncooked rice balls on a tray, then bag. Cook from frozen in boiling water, adding 2 extra minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch of rice balls and freeze for later use.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The mung bean filling can be made a day ahead. Make the dough and cook the balls just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: Flour made from glutinous (sticky) rice. When mixed with water it forms a soft, pliable dough that becomes chewy and translucent when cooked. It is different from regular rice flour.
A sweet syrup made by simmering palm sugar or brown sugar with fresh ginger and water. It is the warming, spiced base for chè trôi nước.

content.text: Chè trôi nước are soft, chewy balls made from
glutinous rice flour
, filled with sweet mung bean paste, and served in a warm
ginger syrup
The balls float to the surface when they are cooked.
This recipe serves 4.
Keep the dough covered with a damp cloth as you work . it dries out quickly. If cracks appear in the rice ball, add a tiny drop of water and smooth with your fingers.
What you need

items.prepNote: use soaked mung beans (100g dried, soaked overnight)

content.text: Method
Make the filling: drain the soaked mung beans and steam or simmer until very soft, about 20 minutes. Mash with the palm sugar until smooth. Roll into 12 small balls about 1 cm across.
Make the syrup: simmer the ginger, brown sugar, and water for 15 minutes. Taste . it should be warmly sweet and fragrant.
Make the coconut cream: heat the coconut milk with the cornflour slurry over low heat, stirring, until slightly thickened. Season with a tiny pinch of seasoning. Keep warm.
Make the dough: mix the glutinous rice flour with enough warm water to form a soft, smooth dough. It should not stick to your hands. Add water a teaspoon at a time if too dry.

Pull off a piece of dough about the size of a walnut. Flatten into a disc. Place a mung bean ball in the centre. Wrap the dough around it, pressing to seal. Roll between your palms to form a smooth ball. Repeat.
Bring a large pan of water to the boil. Cook the rice balls in batches for 4 to 5 minutes. They will float to the surface when cooked. Remove with a slotted spoon.
Ladle the warm ginger syrup into bowls. Add 3 rice balls per person. Drizzle with coconut cream. Serve straight away.

attrs.symptom: The rice balls crack and fall apart in the boiling water.
attrs.cause: The dough was too dry or the balls were not sealed properly.
attrs.fix: Keep the dough moist. Seal each ball carefully by pinching and rolling smooth. Avoid cracks in the surface before cooking.

attrs.symptom: The rice balls are very sticky and hard to handle.
attrs.fix: Dust your hands lightly with a little extra glutinous rice flour. Add the water gradually so you do not over-wet the dough.

attrs.symptom: The filling leaks out during cooking.
attrs.cause: The mung bean ball was too large for the dough or the seal was weak.
attrs.fix: Keep the filling ball small - no more than 1 cm. Make sure the dough is thick enough to enclose it without any gaps.

content.text: Where this dish lives
Chè trôi nước is eaten across Vietnam as a festive and everyday dessert.
It is particularly associated with the Đông Chí winter solstice festival in northern Vietnam.
The dish shows clear Chinese influence through its resemblance to tangyuan.
Vietnamese cooks added their own flavours with palm sugar and pandan.
It is sold at chè stalls throughout the country and is made at home for family occasions.
